question.problem:
A pharmacologist measured $5$ particular features, ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{5},$ for each drug among a group of potential treatments for high blood pressure. The collected data was stored in the standardized observation matrix $X,$ where each row contains measurements for a particular drug.
The singular values of $X$ are 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=6,\,{\sigma }_{2}=3,\,{\sigma }_{3}=2,\,{\sigma }_{4}=1.5,\,{\sigma }_{5}=1.
$$

The pharmacologist then converted the original observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ using the equation $Y=X{V}_{1},$ where ${V}_{1}$ is the $5\times 1$ matrix consisting of the first principal component of the data. What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix $Y$ compared to the initial observation matrix $X?$
question.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

$$
Y=XV
$$

we can convert our observation matrix $X$ into a new matrix $Y$ of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of $Y$ is diagonal (meaning that the new features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are uncorrelated),

- the features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}$ are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

- the squares of the singular values ${\sigma }_{1}^{2},{\sigma }_{2}^{2},…,{\sigma }_{5}^{2}$ represent the variances in the respective features ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{5}.$

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Total} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{5}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(6)^{2}+(3)^{2}+(2)^{2}+(1.5)^{2}+(1)^{2} \\  & =52.25\end{aligned}
$$

Since the researcher used only the first principal component, the remaining variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Remaining} & ∝{\sum }_{i=1}^{1}{\sigma }_{i}^{2} \\  & =(6)^{2} \\  & =36.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{Remaining}}{\text{Total}} & =\frac{36}{52.25} \\  & ≈0.689 \\  & =68.9%.\end{aligned}
$$
